claim: An act is handed a world that lays the kept edits over the checkout, and `rename-page` decides where a folder lands by reading the checkout directly instead. So a second rename drafted onto a first cannot see where the first put the folder: it finds nothing at that path, reads the page as owning no folder, and leaves the folder under its old name. Nothing refuses this. The act answers, the edits are kept, and the folder is wrong. `move-folder` reads the same world through `world.under` and is right, which is what makes the fault hard to see: two acts in one batch disagree about the same tree.

evidence:
`change/modules/page-renaming/page-renaming.module.code.ts` calls `filesIn(world.root, folder)` inside `landingIn`, and `page/naming/modules/folder-named/folder-named.module.code.ts` calls `filesIn(root, at)` inside `namesAbove` and `foldersUnder`. `filesIn` is a `readdirSync` on the checkout. Every other reach in `pageRenamed` goes through the world: `world.textOf`, `world.under`, `world.index`.

Read at HEAD on 2026-09-14. Renaming `design-interfaces` to `design-interface` and then, in the same kept batch, `design-interfaces-badges` to `design-interface-badge`, the second draft answered `moves design/interface/design-interfaces-badges/design-interfaces-badges.domain.ts to design/interface/design-interfaces-badges/design-interface-badge.domain.ts` — the page renamed, the folder not. The folder should have become `badge`: the rule strips the name the folder above says, the folder above is `design-interface` after the first rename, and `design-interface-badge` stripped of `design-interface` is `badge`. `ownsIn` never got that far, because `filesIn` found nothing at `design/interface/design-interfaces-badges` — that path exists only in the overlay — and `ownsIn` answers false for a folder holding no files.

The workaround, and it is a good one: draft `move-folder` after the rename, in the same batch. It reads the overlay, so it finds what the rename put there and moves it where the rule says. The eight renames of the `design-interface` family land as one fold that way.

Why this is wider than stacked renames. Any act reading the disk while its siblings read the overlay is right for as long as no sibling has moved what it reads, and nothing anywhere refuses it for reading the wrong tree. The reading is correct on every change of one act, which is nearly every change, so the fault waits for the batch that stacks two.

The condition a mend would meet: an act reads the tree only through the world it is handed, so what it sees is the tree as the edits kept before it leave it.
